o: Injecting SQL by manipulating server-side variables
Making the server send HTTP requests to arbitrary destinations on the attacker's behalf
Stealing session cookies by forging a server response
Overriding server-side input validation via HTTP headers
questions.x: In SSRF, the attacker controls a URL that the server fetches. The server makes the request from its own network, potentially reaching internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or admin interfaces that are not exposed to the internet.
questions.h: The name has three parts: server-side, request, and forgery. The server is the one being made to send a request somewhere. Who decides where?

questions.q: Why did a direct SSRF attempt to http://192.168.0.12:8080/admin fail in this lab?
o: The internal server does not respond to HTTP
The application has a URL filter that blocks direct internal IP addresses
The admin interface only accepts HTTPS
Port 8080 is blocked by the server firewall
questions.x: The stockApi parameter is filtered. Direct internal addresses like 192.168.x.x are blocked. The open redirection bypass works because the filter only checks the initial URL, not the destination after a redirect.
questions.h: The filter is checking something about the URL you submit. What does it check, and what does it miss when the server follows a redirect?

questions.q: What is an open redirection vulnerability?
o: An endpoint that exposes the Referer header
An endpoint that redirects to a URL supplied by the user without validating the destination
A CORS misconfiguration that allows cross-origin redirects
An HTTP 301 that uses a relative rather than absolute path
questions.x: An open redirect accepts a user-controlled destination URL and issues an HTTP redirect there without checking whether the destination is safe. Chained with SSRF, it lets an attacker route the server to any internal address.
questions.h: The key word is open: the redirect destination is open to whoever requests it. What is the validation step that is missing?

questions.q: Which endpoint contained the open redirect in this lab?
o: /admin/delete
/product?productId=
/product/nextProduct?path=
/stockApi?url=
questions.x: The /product/nextProduct endpoint accepts a path parameter and redirects to it. Providing an internal URL for the path parameter causes the server to follow the redirect when processing the stockApi chain.
questions.h: The endpoint is designed to navigate to the next product. It takes a target URL as a parameter and redirects there. Look for one that explicitly accepts a destination URL.

questions.q: How was the open redirect chained with SSRF in the actual exploit?
o: The stockApi parameter was set to the internal IP directly
The stockApi was set to the redirect endpoint with path= pointing to the internal admin URL
A second request was sent manually to the internal server after the first
The Referer header was forged to include the internal IP
questions.x: stockApi=/product/nextProduct?path=http://192.168.0.12:8080/admin. The filter sees a relative-looking path and allows it. The server follows the redirect to the internal admin URL that the filter would have blocked directly.
questions.h: The filter checks the stockApi value. If you point it at an internal URL via the redirect endpoint, what does the filter see initially versus what the server actually fetches?

o: SSRF that only works on localhost (127.0.0.1)
SSRF where the server makes the request but the response is not returned to the attacker
SSRF that only targets HTTPS endpoints
SSRF exploited without any browser interaction
questions.x: In blind SSRF, the server fetches the URL but the response stays on the server side. The attacker infers success through out-of-band signals like DNS lookups, timing differences, or error messages.
questions.h: Blind means you cannot see the response. How would you know the SSRF worked if you cannot read what the server fetched?

questions.q: Which internal URL was targeted in the lab to solve it?
o: http://localhost/admin
http://10.0.0.1/admin
http://metadata.internal/admin
questions.x: The stock check feature is designed to call an internal inventory service. The lab's admin interface lives at http://192.168.0.12:8080/admin, accessible only from the server's internal network.
questions.h: Private IP ranges include 10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, and 192.168.x.x. The lab uses one of these ranges.

questions.q: Why does the server follow redirects automatically in this scenario?
o: It is configured to mirror all requests to internal mirrors
HTTP client libraries follow redirects by default when fetching URLs
The internal server forces a redirect on the first request
The filter explicitly instructs the server to follow redirects
questions.x: Most HTTP client libraries (curl, Python requests, Java HttpClient) follow 3xx redirects automatically unless disabled. The server-side code fetching the stockApi URL inherits this default behavior.
questions.h: When you use curl or a browser to visit a URL that returns 302, what happens automatically? Server-side HTTP clients work the same way.

questions.q: What category of service is particularly at risk from SSRF attacks in cloud environments?
o: The application's own public API
The cloud instance metadata service (e.g., http://169.254.169.254)
Public CDN endpoints
External payment gateways
questions.x: Cloud metadata services like AWS EC2 metadata at 169.254.169.254 return sensitive data including IAM credentials when fetched from within the instance. SSRF can extract cloud credentials and lead to full account compromise.
questions.h: Cloud providers expose a special link-local address accessible only from within the instance. What does it return that could be catastrophic if leaked?

questions.q: What is the most thorough fix for the SSRF-via-open-redirect chain?
o: Block all requests to port 8080
Validate the initial URL and block redirects to private IP ranges at the HTTP client level
Require authentication on the internal admin panel
Remove the stockApi parameter from the application
questions.x: Fixing only the initial URL filter is not enough when the server follows redirects. The HTTP client must also validate redirect destinations against the same allowlist, blocking any redirect that leads to a private IP range.
questions.h: There are two points where the server could catch this: the initial URL and the redirect destination. Which fix addresses both?
